item.title: Systemic change and EA: What is it all about?
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 6:06 AM GMT

Ever felt like something's missing from how EA talks about “doing good”? Like the conversation stops just short of asking what's actually broken at the root? This opening post introduces a sequence born from exactly that itch: a group of EA-adjacent volunteers who spent three years exploring whether there are systems-level dynamics and interventions that the community should be paying more attention to. 

Post 1: In this first post of our sequence, we set the stage for the empirical and conceptual work to come:  we outline who we are, how our collaboration came about, why we believe systemic change should be more of a focus area within EA and what we are hoping to achieve with this sequence. We hope you consider this as an invitation into an ongoing conversation.

In the coming posts, we will then:

Post 2: Bedazzle you with definitions – what even is “systemic change”?

In the second post of the sequence, we propose an understanding of systemic change-related work that emerged from our internal discussions. Based on that, we outline key criteria that organisations should pay attention to when designing systems-conscious strategies. We offer these as a starting point for discussion across the community and for adaptation by each individual organisation or project.  

Post 3: Excite you with data – do EA organisations actually pay attention to systemic issues already?

In the third post, we describe our empirical investigation. We conducted this in the form of a questionnaire to assess the systems-orientation of existing organisations. We will go into detail on our methodology, present the results from our empirical exercise, and discuss several limitations which reduce the robustness of our findings. 

Post 4: Share our joy and frustration with you – and imagine the future together.

We pick up on these limitations in the last post of the sequence. This post collects open questions, remaining uncertainties, and potential points of contention that we would love to see discussed across the EA community. We close the post with the motivation that started the whole project: our case for an EA-inspired effort to change systems rather than just addressing isolated problems.

Why focus on systemic change?

The case for focusing on the transformation of systems rather than aiming for incremental improvements within a system can be mapped onto cause prioritisation frameworks like ITN or cost-effectiveness analyses, with a slight twist:

Importance

Tackling systemic features that lie at the root of pressing problems is highly important, because such systemic features are often huge levers for improvement. For instance, removing lead from gasoline, water sources, or paint products is a higher-leverage intervention than treating diseases and cognitive impairments after populations have been exposed to lead. Preventing new lead from entering drinking water and other everyday products through changed laws and regulations has even more potential positive impact. At the deepest systemic level, eliminating problems like lead exposure would be achieved most effectively if there were not just new rules but a shift in what societies consider acceptable risks to impose on others. That kind of shift renders it inconceivable for actors to recklessly contaminate living environments in the first place.

Tractability

Tackling systemic issues successfully is moderately tractable. It is true that systems are difficult to understand and predict. Thus, effective interventions are less tractable than they would be for more well-contained, experiment-prone problems. But there are cases of tractable work to promote systemic change. To take just two examples:

  1. Survey research helps to assess the likely success of different mobilisation strategies that social movements use to push for systemic change (Ostarek et al. 2026, Ostarek et al. 2024).
  2. Cash transfer experiments generate evidence about how people might respond if our social and economic system were complemented by Universal Basic Income programmes (GiveDirectly research summary, GiveDirectly list of studies). 

Neglectedness

Tackling systemic issues is ... possibly neglected? We as the authors of this group share an anecdotal sense that this is the case, especially within and adjacent to the EA ecosystem. Our empirical investigation (read Post 3 of the sequence, forthcoming) gestures in a similar direction: It seems like EA-adjacent organisations consider systemic issues mainly in passing and rarely as their main strategy for impact. But that investigation faced major limitations and is not robust enough to turn our results into strong claims. If you disagree on the neglectedness point, we would love to hear from you down in the comments! 

Sustainability?

All that said, we believe that the case for a stronger orientation towards systemic change also carries a benefit which is a bit awkward to fit into the ITN framework (and similar cause prioritisation frameworks): An effective change to a systemic structure is sustainable in a way that one-off interventions often cannot be. Even if interventions addressing the symptoms of a problem might perform well on a cost-effectiveness analysis in the short term, their impact might be short-lived. Problems come back when the intervention is scaled back. The flip side to that is that systemic change must be carefully evaluated to prevent sustained negative change that is hard to reverse.  

Looking at systemic change with the help of these criteria (importance, tractability, neglectedness, and sustained impact) suggests that there is more room in the EA ecosystem for approaches that lead to radical change of systems. We advocate for more research and entrepreneurial attempts to further our understanding of how this could be realised and will propose a long-list of solution directions in the final post of this series.

Who are “we”?

We write these posts as private individuals, not as representatives of any of the organisations we are each affiliated with. This project was not backed by any funding and is purely based on volunteer work. We have different levels of engagement with the effective altruism community, but we all share a commitment to the basic principle of using reasoning and evidence to tackle the world’s problems effectively. We also all believe that the effective altruism community has built an impressive space to flesh out, discuss, and act on this principle.

How did we get here?

The idea for this project emerged through many informal conversations. We had these amongst ourselves, with colleagues who collaborated on the project in its earlier phases, and with others in the EA space (at conferences and other social events). In these conversations, we noticed that we shared a sense of dissatisfaction and confusion about the lack of connections between the EA community and other political and social movements. Many such movements are motivated by similar goals: reduce suffering and increase “moral goods” in the world. But they are often informed by quite different ideas about how to achieve them. More specifically, there is one perspective that seems less prominent in EA than in other movements for doing good. Why focus on systemic change?

Importance

Tackling systemic features that lie at the root of pressing problems is highly important, because such systemic features are often huge levers for improvement. Tackling systemic issues successfully is moderately tractable. It is true that systems are difficult to understand and predict. item.title: New Research: Climate Mitigation is Overlooked by EA
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 2:48 PM GMT

Disclaimer: This blog post focuses on a new piece of research from Rethink Priorities. I was not involved with the funding or execution of this research, and therefore write this piece merely as a consumer. However, I am the Executive Director of Giving Green and a board member of Rethink Priorities, and acknowledge that these affiliations may bias my interpretation of the work. 

 

TL;DR

  • New research from Rethink Priorities seeks to compare cost-effectiveness of high-impact giving in climate change mitigation versus global health and development.
  • Key research contribution is re-calculating the social cost of carbon using an EA-aligned value framework, which allows direct comparison of climate giving opportunities to Coefficient Giving’s (CG) funding bar
  • Conclusion is that donating to high-impact climate funds (such as Giving Green or the Founder’s Pledge Climate Fund) is competitive with Coefficient Giving’s Global Health and Wellbeing Fund, especially given the recent drop in CG’s funding bar
  • Many conversations with AI lab employees lead me to believe that climate is not a priority cause area for this group. As opposed to many other EA-aligned cause areas, I think that climate mitigation is unlikely to be saturated by the hypothetical flood of AI-fueled donations. Therefore, it is likely to become relatively even more cost-effective compared to traditional EA causes. 

 

Introduction

Over time, there have been numerous discussions on how climate change mitigation should rank as an EA cause. For instance, in his influential Climate Change and Longtermism, John Halsted writes, “In my view, climate change is one of the most important problems in the world, but other problems, including engineered viruses, advanced artificial intelligence and nuclear war, are more pressing on the margin because they are so neglected.”

That being said, many donors have a near-to-medium term view and therefore may be directly comparing donating to climate mitigation (for instance, through the Giving Green Fund or the Founder’s Pledge Climate Fund) to global health and development (GHD) options such as giving through Coefficient Giving’s Global Health and Wellbeing (GHW) Fund or Givewell’s (GW) Top Charities Fund. Yet until recently (to my knowledge) there was no quantitative work doing this cross-cause comparison. 

That’s why I was delighted to see new research from Rethink Priorities (Clare and Vargas 2026) that seeks to quantitatively compare the cost-effectiveness of GHW interventions to climate mitigation, specifically by comparing the benchmark of 1-2 dollars/tCO2e sought by the climate funds to the “funding bar” of Coefficient Giving/Givewell. The crux of this comparison lies in the calculation of the “social cost of carbon” (SCC), or the amount of societal damage caused by a ton of CO2 emissions. The findings: climate donations are competitive with GHD, and are more cost-effective than GHD under certain sets of assumptions. This is particularly true now that Coefficient Giving has lowered their funding bar by roughly half, due to “growing expectations of future giving” (presumably from AI Lab employees). 

 

How to compare climate to GHW: Use SROI

When comparing climate mitigation to GHW, Rethink’s approach is to calculate the social return on investment (SROI) of climate funds, and compare it to CG’s funding bar. For CG, their “funding bar” is expressed explicitly as an SROI. In the Rethink paper, CG’s funding bar is stated as 2000x, but CG recently updated it to 1000x. In other words, they expect that for every dollar granted, they will get (in expectation) 1000 dollars worth of value (which could come from saving lives, improving health, improving impact, etc.) Since CG attempts to fund GW until their funding bars are equal, we can assume 1000x to be a good approximation of GW’s marginal funding SROI. 

To calculate the SROI of climate interventions, the authors use two parameters:

  1. Cost effectiveness of climate philanthropy, expressed as the amount of USD required to reduce a tonne of emissions ($/tCO2e)
  2. Social Cost of Carbon (SCC), which is the total cost (including lives lost, economic damage, etc), expressed in $/tCO2e

The ratio of (2) to (1) gives the amount of societal benefit from spending a dollar on climate philanthropy. For instance, if philanthropic opportunities can be bought for $1/tonne, and the SCC is $200/tonne, then the SROI of this investment is 200x. 

To estimate the cost-effectiveness of climate philanthropy, Rethink takes the approach of drawing from a distribution spanning  $.50 and $3.50 (cost per tonne of CO2e avoided). Cost-effectiveness estimates in this space are highly uncertain, but Giving Green’s modeling suggests that opportunities exist at around $1/tonne, and we use this as a rough benchmark when assessing grantmaking opportunities. The prospect of $1/tonne also surfaced in Rethink’s research, as quoted below:

“In our conversations and research, multiple individuals expressed confidence in being able to find interventions at a cost of roughly $1/tonne or even lower. However, because we maintain significant uncertainty about how realistically these opportunities might scale, we wanted to apply a reasonable, perhaps slightly conservative, lean to our abatement costs.”

 

The Key Parameter: Social Cost of Carbon

The most difficult parameter in making this comparison is the social cost of carbon, which is hotly debated in the climate literature. Therefore, Rethink makes the comparison for different assumptions of SCC. 

One issue with using SCCs from the literature is that they rely on assumptions that are standard in the economics literature, such as a modest discount rate. However, these assumptions invalidate a direct comparison to the CG bar. In my mind, the biggest contribution of the Rethink paper is the recalculation of a prominent SCC using “an EA valuation framework” that makes it comparable to the CG bar. This involves changing four main inputs into the SCC:

  • Assuming equal valuation of lives/Disability-Avoided-Life Years (DALYs) globally
  • Application of “pure rate of time preference” of zero (compared to the status quo discount rate of 2%)
  • Weighting of damages such that X dollars of loss are weighted higher for poor people than for rich people. (This is based on CG’s assumption of logarithmic utility, explained here.)
  • Integrating estimated deaths from air pollution, which are not incorporated into standard climate damage models. 

These adjustments, along with some other minor ones, make a meaningful difference. A frequently-cited SCC from Rennert el at (2022) is $185/tonne, which was used by the Biden EPA. However, the adjustments of applying the “EA Evaluation Framework” cause the SCC to rise to over $2000/tonne.

Main Results

The paper’s results explore how the comparison between climate and GHD shifts under a number of assumptions, of which I highlight a couple that I think are most relevant. The first is a simple comparison of the CG bar to the “mainstream” adjusted SCC. This mainstream SCC ($2000/ton, discussed above) accounts for the impact of lives lost, as well as economic impacts from agriculture and sea-level rise. I reproduce this comparison from the Rethink paper below:

 

Adopted from Clare and Vargas (2026). New CG Bar added to graph

Under the old CG bar, CG investments were roughly 2.5x more impactful than climate investments, though the error bars overlapped. However, the new CG bar is very close to the climate SROI, well within the estimates’ range of uncertainty. 

A primary criticism of “mainstream” approaches to SCC such as Rennert et al. (2022) is that they assume exogenous growth and then model economic damages as a percentage of GDP. In other words, the models allow climate to affect levels of GDP, but not growth. This “levels not growth” assumption of standard models has been strongly criticized by many prominent economists, who find it unbelievable that the major societal shifts brought on by climate change will not affect growth. 

If we do assume that climate change affects growth, this massively increases SCC. The Rethink paper surveys the literature on economic growth effects of SCC and finds quite a range of estimates, so they present a few outcomes, shown below. Adopted from Clare and Vargas (2026). New CG Bar added to graph

With economic growth (as well as a modest 25% adjustment for “tipping points”) added to the SCC, climate interventions now easily beat the CG bar. Depending on the assumptions around growth, climate is roughly 2-5x more impactful than CG’s new bar. 

 

Why might this be wrong?

The comparison of climate to GHW is based on quite a few assumptions, which may drive incorrect answers. Critically, both key parameters—cost-effectiveness of climate philanthropy and the social cost of carbon—come with great uncertainty. 

At Giving Green, we do a lot of modeling of the cost-effectiveness of climate donation opportunities, and I will be the first to admit that the modeling is very uncertain. Most of the organizations we support have long theories of change involving policy and/or technology change. Therefore, the models come with many assumptions that could be incorrect. However, we have seen many opportunities that pencil out in the $1/tonne range, making us feel more comfortable that this is an achievable threshold. 

Additionally, the social cost of carbon is a difficult-to-calculate parameter that comes with substantial uncertainty. Complex systems, such as behavior of ice melt from glaciers, and the earth’s changing reflectivity, could have large human effects that are not incorporated in current damage models. Additionally, it is very hard to predict how human adaptation and technological progress will allow society to adapt to changing temperatures. 

Given these fundamental uncertainties in climate philanthropy, donating to climate is definitely more uncertain than donating to GiveWell Top Charities. It is probably more uncertain than donating to GW “all grants” or CG’s GHW fund, but this is less clear because some of the grants made from these funds also rely on uncertain theories of change, such as policy change. 

 

Conclusion

Many in the EA community tend to believe that donations to climate organizations are not competitive with other near- or medium-termist opportunities. This new research shows that is not clearly the case, and that climate appears competitive with EA-aligned GHD options such as Givewell. 

In the near term, cause areas traditionally favored by EA (such as GHD) are expecting a flood of money, which will likely saturate grantmakers, and reduce the marginal cost-effectiveness of additional contributions. We see this dynamic already, with CG recently lowering its funding bar by half (from an SROI of 2000x to 1000x). 

This dynamic is unlikely to affect climate grantmaking in the same way. Many conversations have led me to believe that climate is not a priority cause area among most early AI lab employees, meaning it is unlikely that the anticipated upcoming wave of philanthropy will saturate climate funds the same way it will other causes. Therefore, I think climate will remain cost-effective on the margin, and over time will become relatively more attractive in comparison with other favored EA causes. 

As of now, EA-aligned climate grantmaking is far from saturated. Over at Giving Green, we have built up a 6-person research and grantmaking function, and are on track to make ~34 million in new grants from the Giving Green Fund in 2026. Much of this grantmaking is fueled by a large gift we received in 2025, and we are on track to meet our goal of completely regranting this large gift, as well as all other assets currently in our fund, by the end of 2026. This leaves us with plenty of grantmaking capacity for late 2026 and 2027- we think at our current staffing levels we could make 100M of grants in 2027, and could also increase staffing to create more capacity.

Many in the EA community tend to believe that donations to climate organizations are not competitive with other near- or medium-termist opportunities. This new research shows that is not clearly the case, and that climate appears competitive with EA-aligned GHD options such as Givewell. 

In the near term, cause areas traditionally favored by EA (such as GHD) are expecting a flood of money, which will likely saturate grantmakers, and reduce the marginal cost-effectiveness of additional contributions. We see this dynamic already, with CG recently lowering its funding bar by half (from an SROI of 2000x to 1000x). 

This dynamic is unlikely to affect climate grantmaking in the same way. Many conversations have led me to believe that climate is not a priority cause area among most early AI lab employees, meaning it is unlikely that the anticipated upcoming wave of philanthropy will saturate climate funds the same way it will other causes. Therefore, I think climate will remain cost-effective on the margin, and over time will become relatively more attractive in comparison with other favored EA causes. 

As of now, EA-aligned climate grantmaking is far from saturated. Over at Giving Green, we have built up a 6-person research and grantmaking function, and are on track to make ~34 million in new grants from the Giving Green Fund in 2026. Much of this grantmaking is fueled by a large gift we received in 2025, and we are on track to meet our goal of completely regranting this large gift, as well as all other assets currently in our fund, by the end of 2026. This leaves us with plenty of grantmaking capacity for late 2026 and 2027- we think at our current staffing levels we could make 100M of grants in 2027, and could also increase staffing to create more capacity.

item.title: Two crazy-ish charitable global poverty project ideas
item.description:
Published on August 18, 2026 9:54 PM GMT

I am writing up two charity ideas I’ve wanted to investigate, but haven’t been able to, in the hopes someone will investigate them further. If you end up investigating either, I'd be most interested to see what conclusions you come to!

Vulture preservation as a global health intervention

Since the mid 1990's the vulture population in India has been rapidly declining. The reason is due to a few chemicals which are fed to livestock, which is highly poisonous to vultures.

A paper by two University of Chicago economists came to the surprising conclusion that the decline of vultures increased human mortality by 4% (!!) leading to hundreds of thousands of excess deaths. That number peaked my attention.

After reading it, I reached out to the authors of the paper as well as some people working on vulture preservation in India to learn more.

My takeaway (this was almost two years ago, so my memory is fuzzy) was that the chemicals responsible for the decline of vultures (particularly diclofenac) had cheap alternatives and that lethargy alongside regulation imposing minor switching costs to industry has kept regulation from being taken up and enforced.

By doing LEEP style policy advocacy to adopt and enforce bans on the chemicals responsible for the die-out, one might be able to save many lives. The project would be to find out what regulation is needed, lobby to get it passed, and then lobby to ensure it is enforced.

It’s likely also possible to raise money for this project from conservationists who usually spend their money on things I don’t value much, therefore vastly increasing the counterfactual impact (insofar as you as you share my ethics).

Further research that is needed:

  1. Learning exactly what chemicals are responsible for the vulture die out, which alternatives exist, switching costs, and so forth
  2. Regulatory hurdles. Would a ban instituted at a state or national level? Do such bans already exist? If so are they enforced? If not, why? Any low hanging fruit?
  3. CEA with BOTECs of the value of vulture restoration, campaign costs, chance of campaign success, costs to industry and government, time discounts, and so forth.
  4. A critical read of the study to decide if the excess death estimate holds water, and a projection of how this number extrapolates into the future. My expectation is that widespread improvements to sanitation in India over the last decade would make the effect size much smaller going forward.

Radio infotainment on responsible income planning in developing countries

A recent RCT by Stefan Dercon et al. found that showing people in rural Ethiopia a video of people in similar circumstances to themselves making clever financial and life choices massively increased future-oriented investments down the line compared to people not shown the documentary.

It’s exactly the type of social science study that pattern matches to my “doesn’t replicate” neuron, but the authors of the study are far from idiots and the RCT is well done, and it’s well.. an RCT.

Even with that in mind I think people would be right to feel skeptical of this result. Beware of the man of one study! But there’s another similar result which leads me to believe the RCT really is onto something.

Family Empowerment Media, an AIM incubated charity, creates radio infotainment to encourage contraceptive uptake. Their effect sizes are also totally nutty.

Ever since seeing FEMs results, I’ve wondered:

  1. Is knowledge of contraceptive options / dispelling stigmas & myths highly conducive to behavioral change?
  2. Is infotainment in general just a really really powerful tool to induce behavior change?

This new RCT pushes me over to thinking that it’s probably the case that infotainment is severely neglected as a way to cause behavioral change.

Radio outreach in developing countries is way cheaper than it has any right to be. When people have no money the value of advertising coca-cola is far lower and a juicy arbitrage emerges.

I think there’s a possible charity which develops compelling infotainment on responsible economic planning, which plausibly could become the world’s most cost-effective charity aimed at improving economic conditions.

One possible counterargument is that people have limited attention spans and different infotainment interventions will crowd each other out. Perhaps if you run infotainment about family planning AND financial planning, they start cannibalizing each other's effect sizes.

Whatever gains you see in family planning comes at the expense of financial planning and whatever else you’re informing people about.

IIRC when this was studied in Denmark, it did look like awareness campaigns for eg. driving safely would cause a reduction in traffic accidents, but correspondingly drive up all other causes of mortality.

Nevertheless even if this effect proves significant, there’s a case for pushing down the salience of coca-cola and up the salience of investing in one’s future.

Research questions:

  1. Find an AIM botec of radio interventions and see how they structure their CEAs of radio planning. Estimate effect sizes of radio programming from Stephen Dercon’s RCT and from that create a BOTEC.
  2. Similarly to the vulture intervention, this idea heavily relies on a single study’s results. Beware the man of one study! Do a skeptical evaluation of the whole idea and look for any questionable assumptions.
  3. Speak to FEM’s leadership, ask simple questions like: “what infotainment has FEM found to work best?”, “Do you have one with subtitles I can watch?”.

 

 

Side note: I found this post sitting in my drafts and realized I never got around to completing it. I'm now posting it despite it being much below the quality of writing I usually feel good putting out. If you found this write up worthwhile to read, that's useful feedback for me to lower my bar for what I post.

item.title: WAI is starting Phase 3 of field-building for wild animal welfare science
item.description:
Published on August 19, 2026 9:49 AM GMT

Summary

This post will summarize the trajectory of Wild Animal Initiative’s field-building for wild animal welfare science so far, along with patterns and indicators we want to see more of going forward. Beginning with an initial phase focused on establishing credibility and awareness of the field, through a second phase that has placed more emphasis on the distinctiveness and broad priorities of the field, we are now moving into a third phase designed to consolidate effort and encourage more projects to build on each other, enabling the field to make faster progress towards answers to key questions and potential interventions. This post also covers where our research funding has gone over the past few years and some of the field-building milestones we’re seeing.

 

WAI’s early field-building

Wild Animal Initiative (WAI) launched in early 2019 with the objective of establishing a mainstream scientific field dedicated to the practical study of wild animal welfare (hereafter referred to as “wild animal welfare science” or WAWS). We chose to approach the problem of wild animal suffering through scientific field-building because there were (and remain) many critical questions requiring empirical research before we could know that any wild animal welfare intervention or policy is having a net-positive impact. The study of wild animal welfare requires concepts, methods and skills from both ecology and animal welfare science, but at the time, there were very few scientists studying the welfare of free-living wild animals and there was little crossover between these fields in terms of projects, conferences, or academic programs. Although it would be possible to hire scientists from one of these fields and cross-train them to do research outside of academia (as indeed we do at Wild Animal Initiative on our research team), academic institutions provide a number of efficiencies, such as access to specialized laboratory equipment, field sites, agreements with publishers, and a culture of peer review. By funding academic research, we could take advantage of expertise and infrastructure all over the world, which would also allow us to reach more animals. By helping to coordinate WAWS into a recognized academic field, we could multiply the impact of the research we fund by making its importance clearer to other scientists and decision-makers, and by potentially attracting mainstream funding from universities and agencies to support more WAWS projects.

Our first challenge was establishing awareness and legitimacy of WAWS as a useful, scientifically compelling and tractable area of research. This would attract scientists from adjacent fields to integrate WAWS concepts and methods into their current research, providing experience that would reveal to them and us their level of enthusiasm and aptitude for long-term engagement with the field.

In those first few years, we emphasized areas of overlap with the adjacent fields of ecology, conservation and captive animal welfare science. We asked researchers in these fields to give WAWS a try. For ecologists that meant trying to interpret physiology and behavior in terms of welfare or measuring putative welfare indicators alongside their population and habitat-scale metrics, while for captive animal welfare scientists that meant developing welfare indicators for species with large wild populations or devising new methods to make captive-based welfare assessment methods feasible to apply in the wild. The support of Coefficient Giving, beginning in 2021, allowed us to launch a grants program and enable many more ecologists and captive animal welfare scientists the opportunity to try their hand at wild animal welfare research. This supercharged our field-building work. Beyond the handful of projects we could actually afford to fund, the prospect of receiving a grant incentivized hundreds more researchers to submit proposals engaging with the concepts and methods we wrote about and collaboratively advised them on.

As we started to see repeat grantees and increasingly relevant projects being proposed, we shifted emphasis away from encouraging researchers to ‘try’ WAWS by simply integrating it with their existing research programs, and increasingly emphasized the challenging priority areas and concerns that make the field distinct and will be necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions. See for example the text of our 2023 call for Seed Grant (<$30k) proposals or our most recent (2025) call for proposals.

As someone who has been with Wild Animal Initiative since the beginning (coming from a PhD in molecular ecology and working part-time on academic outreach at Animal Ethics), if you told me back then that this would be the state of wild animal welfare science in 2026, I would be thrilled. Especially in the past year, we have begun to see important external signals of field-building milestones being reached, including:

  • WAI co-organized the 2025 meeting of the UK’s Animal Welfare Research Network, with approximately a third of the conference dedicated to wild animal welfare. We will be doing something similar for the Spanish-language equivalent, RedCIBA, this year, and have been invited to sponsor themed sessions at several other conferences. WAI’s staff researchers have organized workshops and sessions at many other conferences over the years; what is new here is the scale of our involvement and that we are being invited.
  • WAI’s research team was invited to curate a special issue of the highly regarded journal, Integrative & Comparative Biology, focused on wild animal welfare. This is a huge opportunity and a field-building milestone that they noticed WAI’s research and thought that wild animal welfare would be a compelling theme for their readership.
  • We are seeing more collaborations emerge organically among WAI grantees, and concrete interest in establishing WAWS academic institutions. Within the next six months, we expect to support the launch of the first academic center dedicated to the ecological dimension of wild animal welfare, spearheaded by a cluster of WAI grantees and benefiting from university co-funding. This will complement the NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program, which focuses more on policy analysis. Earlier this year, we also made a grant to Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC) to develop a standalone wild animal welfare module that would connect students from their animal welfare and conservation MSc programs, as well as create a wild animal welfare scholarship and fund small student research projects in wild animal welfare.

Our theory of change has always been centered on academic field-building, as we think that is the only way to get research done at scale with the credibility that will be required to bring positive policy attention to wild animal welfare (on that note, we’re excited to work with the new policy-focused CWAW!). However, academic field-building is only a means to an end, and ultimately we will only be able to improve wild animal welfare if the field produces quality research on impactful welfare issues.

 

The foundation of WAWS laid so far

Developing the science necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions that can meaningfully impact most animals is a huge, long-term endeavor, and most of that impact will be felt only after a sustainable, mission-aligned academic field is established. To that end, we have seen meaningful progress through our grants and internal research towards identifying priorities for further, more concentrated research to focus on. Broadly, we categorize these in terms of identifying factors impacting wild animal welfare, developing tools for assessing wild animal welfare at scale (necessary for monitoring & evaluating interventions), and scoping wild animal welfare interventions. I summarize some highlights from each category here, and you can see the broad sweep of WAI’s external grantmaking allocation in Figure 1 below.

Measuring wild animal welfare

  • Does DNA methylation reflect environmental and social adversity?: This project is taking advantage of detailed biographical information assembled over decades of monitoring a single Rocky Mountains marmot population to test whether DNA methylation (a proxy for biological ageing) correlates with an index of early life adversity. This builds on previous work from this team, developing the index, and connects to the importance of juvenile welfare.
  • Harnessing machine learning for the non-invasive assessment of wild fish welfare: This project builds on a previous WAI-funded project that developed a judgement bias test for juvenile wild fish by combining a similar approach with machine learning to make it more scalable. We hope that scalable wild animal welfare data collection will eventually lead to a ‘passive’ uptake of wild animal welfare into policy decisions (in addition to the effects of active advocacy) simply by making such data available to decision makers. For example, if someone is performing an environmental impact assessment, they will come across evidence of welfare impacts in their  literature searches alongside evidence of population/conservation impacts.
  • Feeling salty: A welfare framework for estuarine fishes: This project aims to identify a specific set of indicators that are both informative and feasible for monitoring the welfare of fish in estuaries. We like that this project is explicitly about making WAWS practicable on the ground and integrating it into environmental impact assessments affecting large numbers of individuals. It’s the kind of project we’ll need to see repeated in many more ecological contexts.
  • Environmental drivers of welfare in urban rats: A multimodal field study of micro-habitat conditions and affective behavior: This project, hosted by Basis.ai, will develop a scalable monitoring platform for rat welfare using indicators validated in captivity. With one of the most promising near-term wild animal welfare interventions being rodent fertility control, this is just the kind of thing we’ll need to be able to monitor and optimize our interventions.
  • Developing an automated cognitive bias task for wild squirrels: This project will transfer a challenging but widely accepted method of welfare assessment in captivity to a wild rodent in a way that emphasizes scalability and cost-effectiveness.
  • Thermal imaging as a non-invasive welfare assessment tool for tracking the impact of environmental stressors across wild animal populations: This project seeks to validate eye temperature as a welfare indicator for wild birds. By using thermal cameras at feeding stations, the method should also be scalable and ideal for monitoring the impact of interventions based around fixed locations, like supplemental feeding or contraceptive bait stations.
  • Developing an approach for assessing the welfare of wild birds through the use of bioacoustics analysis and Assessing animal welfare from bioacoustic monitoring in red-billed choughs: These two similar projects, funded at the same time, are both developing passive acoustic monitoring to study wild bird welfare. This approach could also be automated and scaled at relatively low cost, and used alongside similar approaches, like thermal imaging.
  • Remote welfare assessment in wildlife using stand-off Raman spectroscopy: This project seeks to develop a method for measuring cortisol levels in the hair of wild mammals remotely, using Raman spectroscopy. Although cortisol is not the strongest welfare indicator by itself, the prospect of measuring it without even touching an animal provides great potential for large-scale automated welfare monitoring in combination with things like camera traps, thermal imaging and bioacoustics.
  • Developing, testing and validating indicators of wild insect welfare: This project will attempt to validate a suite of field-accessible welfare indicators for three common yet disparate insect species. Meghan Barrett of the Insect Welfare Research Society is also a collaborator.

Understanding factors affecting welfare

  • Stranding: a blessing or a curse? Testing assumptions of fish welfare during habitat fragmentation: This project is investigating what happens to welfare when drought separates fish populations into isolated and shrinking lakes. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned PhD student.
  • Evaluating wild animal welfare in landscapes of fear at urban-wildland interfaces: This project is investigating potential welfare impact of lizards’ fear response to suburban dangers, such as vehicles and cats. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned postdoc, and is investigating DNA methylation as a potential welfare indicator.
  • Parasites in the city: How is the impact of parasites on wild animal welfare affected by urbanization?: This project will evaluate the welfare impact of parasitic infections on grey squirrels and relate it to their age and other demographic factors in a QALY-like framework (‘welfare expectancy’).

Welfare interventions

  • Towards welfare-centered prescribed fire: With climate change increasing wildfire risk globally, there is increasing emphasis on forestry tactics such as controlled burns. This project will study how bush rats react to controlled burns and use that information to create welfare-focused guidelines that minimize impacts on wild rodent welfare. These guidelines could also help reduce the wild animal suffering caused by unplanned/naturogenic wildfires.

  • Does diet mediate effects of sublethal parasitic infections on host welfare?: This project is primarily studying the impact of intestinal nematode parasites on wild mouse welfare and how that effect interacts with other risk factors. However, because it takes an experimental approach by deworming some of the mice in expectation of seeing a positive welfare impact, it could also be considered a trial of a wild animal welfare intervention.

     

Figure 1: How WAI’s grantmaking has broken out across taxa (note that rodents are distinguished as a priority group from non-rodent mammals), project types, and welfare factor categories since our 2023 calls for proposals (which is when our metrics became more consistent). It reflects the consequences of some meaningful prioritization decisions on our part: 1) lots of funding to rodent projects; 2) significant funding to invertebrate projects and almost all of it to projects whose primary purpose is "measuring welfare" (because that remains the primary barrier to understanding and improving invertebrate welfare, even more than with other taxa); 3) generally diversified funding across taxa and welfare factors. These reflect our strategy of building and maintaining a broad field that is working towards a better world for all animals, while nudging its priorities towards the most numerous animals and the most important and tractable causes of suffering. Note that for projects that considered welfare factors from multiple categories, the budget was divided equally across those categories.

 

What we haven’t seen enough of

We are happy with the foundation of wild animal welfare research we’ve seeded over the past few years, and excited to see those projects’ results. However, as I alluded to earlier, most of our early grantmaking took a big-tent, experimental approach, emphasizing giving a shot to scientists who were new to the field (which was almost everyone at the beginning) and initiating projects on diverse species using diverse methods. There is necessarily a trade-off, and that brings me to the topic of what we haven’t optimized for up to this point but need to see more of going forward. We haven’t seen enough projects building on each other. I mentioned one standout example above, which is the project using machine learning to evaluate attention bias in wild fish. However, this is one of a handful of exceptions.

The long timescale of academic research is probably a huge factor. From the point when we fund a project, it usually takes months to start; sometimes because the principal investigator must recruit a PhD student or postdoc, or permits must be obtained. Then, the pace of many projects is limited by field seasons. Once the data is collected, the pace of analysis and writing is largely in the hands of the researchers, but it is challenging, often requiring coordination of a whole team of researchers who may have other projects or teaching responsibilities. Then, there’s the academic publishing process, which is genuinely inefficient (to put it mildly). The net result of this is that most of the projects WAI has funded have not published their results yet, and the ones that have are mostly from the earliest funding rounds, when we funded projects on the widest variety of themes and methods. Funding wide early was a strategic choice, since our first priority was introducing new people to the field and demonstrating its scope and relevance across many disciplines. However, all this means that there has been little opportunity for new grant applicants to build on or even learn about previous WAI-funded research unless they already collaborate with the relevant grantees. Moreover, each year we’ve received a larger share of projects focusing on abundant/neglected taxa and more important causes of suffering, and we’ve generally prioritized those over continuing to fund less impactful research directions. We’re really pleased to be seeing that shift and think we’ve taken the right approach so far, but we are approaching a pivot point. Ultimately, it is crucial for projects to build on each other and develop into deep research programs because actually improving wild animal welfare is such a complex, multi-step challenge.

  

The next phase of WAI’s strategy

If our initial priority of establishing mainstream acceptance of WAWS was phase 1 of WAI’s strategy (~2019-2023), and phase 2 involved emphasizing the distinctiveness of the field by leaning more into our priority themes while still focusing on growing the field (~2023-26), we are now entering a third phase. To accelerate progress improving wild animal welfare by building on this initial foundation of research initiatives, and to encourage long-term commitment to WAWS by reinvesting in the researchers who have demonstrated enthusiasm and aptitude for WAWS, the next phase of WAI’s strategy will emphasize the development of research programs over individual projects, and developing institutions through networks of researchers.

We have lots of plans and changes in store to address those objectives. I won’t share anything here that we aren’t prepared to share with the scientists in our network, but I can describe some of the most important changes that will be coming to our grants program when our next call for proposals launches this fall. Currently, we offer three main types of research grants that are primarily distinguished by their budget limits and competitiveness. We are now introducing all-new grant types, with much more specific purposes. These grant types will be offered simultaneously, but are designed to lead from one type to the next for any given research program or study system:

  • The first stage will be a Seed Grant (<$30k), which are for observational or pilot studies intended to identify candidate welfare indicators that could be subjected to a more rigorous validation experiment. For example, I have rescued dozens of injured garden snails, and I’ve noticed a few things that might be relevant to welfare: the posture and rigidity of their eye stalks seems to vary depending on the circumstances, and how much they retract their body into their shells when they sleep seems to vary among individuals. Those hypotheses aren’t developed or grounded enough to warrant a validation experiment, but with a Seed Grant I could quantify those snail behaviors alongside welfare-relevant conditions (such as competition or parasite load) to look for statistical associations as a first step. (Incidentally, we recently funded a welfare indicator validation project for snails!)
  • For better-understood taxa and contexts, a Seed Grant may not be necessary and a researcher can proceed directly to the first major grant type, a Validation Grant (<$200k). These projects will be entirely focused on testing the validity of potential welfare indicators through a structured process originally proposed by Heather Browning and applied by WAI’s Research Manager Michaël Beaulieu and others (e.g. Beaulieu 2024). The validation process is absolutely essential for truly understanding wild animal welfare because it confirms that we are actually assessing welfare. However, it is highly rigorous, and we’ve found that many grant applicants understandably want to skip ahead to the more interesting and motivating questions. That’s why we’re introducing a specific grant type dedicated to this kind of project.
  • We are also tightening our requirements for projects’ welfare assessment frameworks, which will give grantees who successfully deliver on a validation project a distinct advantage if they subsequently propose to address those more interesting questions via the next grant type, a Welfare Ecology Grant (<$200k). These grants will focus on assessing how wild animal welfare is affected by ecological factors, such as resource availability, disease, etc., within particular ecosystems. The objective of these grants is to gradually build up a picture of the causal network of factors so that interventions or policies can eventually be devised to improve wild animal welfare.
  • Intervention Grants will support that final step, and will debut next year, with our 2027 call for proposals. These projects will run field trials of interventions based on justified hypotheses and monitoring and evaluation tools of the sort developed through Validation Grants and Welfare Ecology Grants. Currently, we do not have these pieces in place for any wild animal welfare intervention, although we have funded projects working towards a foundation for testing a few potential interventions, including rodent fertility control and bird feeding. Between now and the launch of Intervention Grants, WAI’s research team will also be developing a new internal research agenda for 2027-29 by working backwards from potential wild animal welfare interventions to identify recurring research questions that would need to be answered in order to recommend for or against multiple specific interventions. Our internal research agenda will focus on broad conceptual or methodological questions that emerge, but other lessons from this process will inform what we ask of future Intervention Grant applicants.

 

Figure 2: The progression path through WAI grant types. A grant applicant seeking to break ground on a new research program would first apply for a Seed Grant if their focal species and the welfare challenges they face are poorly understood. If the basic biology of the species is reasonably well understood, but it has not been studied in welfare terms in the wild, they may apply directly for a Validation Grant. If the applicant is already an experienced wild animal welfare scientist (based on publication record) and there are validated indicators for the proposed focal species (or close relatives), they may apply directly for a Welfare Ecology Grant. We expect that it will take multiple Welfare Ecology Grant projects (by the same or different teams) for most research programs to mature to the point where they can proceed to an Intervention Grant.

 

We will also be experimenting with ways to hasten the handover of new knowledge between projects, such as requiring grantees to commit to a timeline for publication (or at least pre-print sharing) and facilitating more small-scale meet-ups for researchers working on related problems (like this one organized by WAI grantees working on applying cognitive bias tests to wild animals). Investing in WAWS institutions, particularly research centers, could also help accelerate research feedback loops, since co-located wild animal welfare scientists should be relatively up-to-date with each other’s findings.

Conclusion

WAI’s first 7 years of field-building for wild animal welfare science has laid the foundations of a recognized and growing field (albeit one still almost fully dependent on WAI for funding). We have prioritized establishing awareness and legitimacy for the field, publishing research that articulates key concepts of the field, and awarding research grants that showcase the scope and priorities of the field while giving scientists from adjacent fields an opportunity to incorporate wild animal welfare into their personal research programs. A trade-off of this approach is that research has been less concentrated towards any single breakthrough or intervention. However, we are already seeing this pay off in terms of a broad base of interest and support for wild animal welfare science. Our grants have seeded many compelling avenues for further development, and we think the field has reached a stage where WAI-funded research effort can become more consolidated into projects that build on one another. By Luke Hecht

Published on August 19, 2026 9:49 AM GMT

Summary

This post will summarize the trajectory of Wild Animal Initiative’s field-building for wild animal welfare science so far, along with patterns and indicators we want to see more of going forward. Beginning with an initial phase focused on establishing credibility and awareness of the field, through a second phase that has placed more emphasis on the distinctiveness and broad priorities of the field, we are now moving into a third phase designed to consolidate effort and encourage more projects to build on each other, enabling the field to make faster progress towards answers to key questions and potential interventions. This post also covers where our research funding has gone over the past few years and some of the field-building milestones we’re seeing.

 

WAI’s early field-building

Wild Animal Initiative (WAI) launched in early 2019 with the objective of establishing a mainstream scientific field dedicated to the practical study of wild animal welfare (hereafter referred to as “wild animal welfare science” or WAWS). We chose to approach the problem of wild animal suffering through scientific field-building because there were (and remain) many critical questions requiring empirical research before we could know that any wild animal welfare intervention or policy is having a net-positive impact. The study of wild animal welfare requires concepts, methods and skills from both ecology and animal welfare science, but at the time, there were very few scientists studying the welfare of free-living wild animals and there was little crossover between these fields in terms of projects, conferences, or academic programs. Although it would be possible to hire scientists from one of these fields and cross-train them to do research outside of academia (as indeed we do at Wild Animal Initiative on our research team), academic institutions provide a number of efficiencies, such as access to specialized laboratory equipment, field sites, agreements with publishers, and a culture of peer review. By funding academic research, we could take advantage of expertise and infrastructure all over the world, which would also allow us to reach more animals. By helping to coordinate WAWS into a recognized academic field, we could multiply the impact of the research we fund by making its importance clearer to other scientists and decision-makers, and by potentially attracting mainstream funding from universities and agencies to support more WAWS projects.

Our first challenge was establishing awareness and legitimacy of WAWS as a useful, scientifically compelling and tractable area of research. This would attract scientists from adjacent fields to integrate WAWS concepts and methods into their current research, providing experience that would reveal to them and us their level of enthusiasm and aptitude for long-term engagement with the field.

In those first few years, we emphasized areas of overlap with the adjacent fields of ecology, conservation and captive animal welfare science. We asked researchers in these fields to give WAWS a try. For ecologists that meant trying to interpret physiology and behavior in terms of welfare or measuring putative welfare indicators alongside their population and habitat-scale metrics, while for captive animal welfare scientists that meant developing welfare indicators for species with large wild populations or devising new methods to make captive-based welfare assessment methods feasible to apply in the wild. The support of Coefficient Giving, beginning in 2021, allowed us to launch a grants program and enable many more ecologists and captive animal welfare scientists the opportunity to try their hand at wild animal welfare research. This supercharged our field-building work. Beyond the handful of projects we could actually afford to fund, the prospect of receiving a grant incentivized hundreds more researchers to submit proposals engaging with the concepts and methods we wrote about and collaboratively advised them on.

As we started to see repeat grantees and increasingly relevant projects being proposed, we shifted emphasis away from encouraging researchers to ‘try’ WAWS by simply integrating it with their existing research programs, and increasingly emphasized the challenging priority areas and concerns that make the field distinct and will be necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions. See for example the text of our 2023 call for Seed Grant (<$30k) proposals or our most recent (2025) call for proposals.

As someone who has been with Wild Animal Initiative since the beginning (coming from a PhD in molecular ecology and working part-time on academic outreach at Animal Ethics), if you told me back then that this would be the state of wild animal welfare science in 2026, I would be thrilled. Especially in the past year, we have begun to see important external signals of field-building milestones being reached, including:

  • WAI co-organized the 2025 meeting of the UK’s Animal Welfare Research Network, with approximately a third of the conference dedicated to wild animal welfare. We will be doing something similar for the Spanish-language equivalent, RedCIBA, this year, and have been invited to sponsor themed sessions at several other conferences. WAI’s staff researchers have organized workshops and sessions at many other conferences over the years; what is new here is the scale of our involvement and that we are being invited.
  • WAI’s research team was invited to curate a special issue of the highly regarded journal, Integrative & Comparative Biology, focused on wild animal welfare. This is a huge opportunity and a field-building milestone that they noticed WAI’s research and thought that wild animal welfare would be a compelling theme for their readership.
  • We are seeing more collaborations emerge organically among WAI grantees, and concrete interest in establishing WAWS academic institutions. Within the next six months, we expect to support the launch of the first academic center dedicated to the ecological dimension of wild animal welfare, spearheaded by a cluster of WAI grantees and benefiting from university co-funding. This will complement the NYU Wild Animal Welfare Program, which focuses more on policy analysis. Earlier this year, we also made a grant to Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC) to develop a standalone wild animal welfare module that would connect students from their animal welfare and conservation MSc programs, as well as create a wild animal welfare scholarship and fund small student research projects in wild animal welfare.

Our theory of change has always been centered on academic field-building, as we think that is the only way to get research done at scale with the credibility that will be required to bring positive policy attention to wild animal welfare (on that note, we’re excited to work with the new policy-focused CWAW!). However, academic field-building is only a means to an end, and ultimately we will only be able to improve wild animal welfare if the field produces quality research on impactful welfare issues.

 

The foundation of WAWS laid so far

Developing the science necessary to inform responsible wild animal welfare interventions that can meaningfully impact most animals is a huge, long-term endeavor, and most of that impact will be felt only after a sustainable, mission-aligned academic field is established. To that end, we have seen meaningful progress through our grants and internal research towards identifying priorities for further, more concentrated research to focus on. Broadly, we categorize these in terms of identifying factors impacting wild animal welfare, developing tools for assessing wild animal welfare at scale (necessary for monitoring & evaluating interventions), and scoping wild animal welfare interventions. I summarize some highlights from each category here, and you can see the broad sweep of WAI’s external grantmaking allocation in Figure 1 below.

Measuring wild animal welfare

  • Does DNA methylation reflect environmental and social adversity?: This project is taking advantage of detailed biographical information assembled over decades of monitoring a single Rocky Mountains marmot population to test whether DNA methylation (a proxy for biological ageing) correlates with an index of early life adversity. This builds on previous work from this team, developing the index, and connects to the importance of juvenile welfare.
  • Harnessing machine learning for the non-invasive assessment of wild fish welfare: This project builds on a previous WAI-funded project that developed a judgement bias test for juvenile wild fish by combining a similar approach with machine learning to make it more scalable. We hope that scalable wild animal welfare data collection will eventually lead to a ‘passive’ uptake of wild animal welfare into policy decisions (in addition to the effects of active advocacy) simply by making such data available to decision makers. For example, if someone is performing an environmental impact assessment, they will come across evidence of welfare impacts in their  literature searches alongside evidence of population/conservation impacts.
  • Feeling salty: A welfare framework for estuarine fishes: This project aims to identify a specific set of indicators that are both informative and feasible for monitoring the welfare of fish in estuaries. We like that this project is explicitly about making WAWS practicable on the ground and integrating it into environmental impact assessments affecting large numbers of individuals. It’s the kind of project we’ll need to see repeated in many more ecological contexts.
  • Environmental drivers of welfare in urban rats: A multimodal field study of micro-habitat conditions and affective behavior: This project, hosted by Basis.ai, will develop a scalable monitoring platform for rat welfare using indicators validated in captivity. With one of the most promising near-term wild animal welfare interventions being rodent fertility control, this is just the kind of thing we’ll need to be able to monitor and optimize our interventions.
  • Developing an automated cognitive bias task for wild squirrels: This project will transfer a challenging but widely accepted method of welfare assessment in captivity to a wild rodent in a way that emphasizes scalability and cost-effectiveness.
  • Thermal imaging as a non-invasive welfare assessment tool for tracking the impact of environmental stressors across wild animal populations: This project seeks to validate eye temperature as a welfare indicator for wild birds. By using thermal cameras at feeding stations, the method should also be scalable and ideal for monitoring the impact of interventions based around fixed locations, like supplemental feeding or contraceptive bait stations.
  • Developing an approach for assessing the welfare of wild birds through the use of bioacoustics analysis and Assessing animal welfare from bioacoustic monitoring in red-billed choughs: These two similar projects, funded at the same time, are both developing passive acoustic monitoring to study wild bird welfare. This approach could also be automated and scaled at relatively low cost, and used alongside similar approaches, like thermal imaging.
  • Remote welfare assessment in wildlife using stand-off Raman spectroscopy: This project seeks to develop a method for measuring cortisol levels in the hair of wild mammals remotely, using Raman spectroscopy. Although cortisol is not the strongest welfare indicator by itself, the prospect of measuring it without even touching an animal provides great potential for large-scale automated welfare monitoring in combination with things like camera traps, thermal imaging and bioacoustics.
  • Developing, testing and validating indicators of wild insect welfare: This project will attempt to validate a suite of field-accessible welfare indicators for three common yet disparate insect species. Meghan Barrett of the Insect Welfare Research Society is also a collaborator.

Understanding factors affecting welfare

  • Stranding: a blessing or a curse? Testing assumptions of fish welfare during habitat fragmentation: This project is investigating what happens to welfare when drought separates fish populations into isolated and shrinking lakes. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned PhD student.
  • Evaluating wild animal welfare in landscapes of fear at urban-wildland interfaces: This project is investigating potential welfare impact of lizards’ fear response to suburban dangers, such as vehicles and cats. It is also a fellowship for a mission-aligned postdoc, and is investigating DNA methylation as a potential welfare indicator.
  • Parasites in the city: How is the impact of parasites on wild animal welfare affected by urbanization?: This project will evaluate the welfare impact of parasitic infections on grey squirrels and relate it to their age and other demographic factors in a QALY-like framework (‘welfare expectancy’).

Welfare interventions

  • Towards welfare-centered prescribed fire: With climate change increasing wildfire risk globally, there is increasing emphasis on forestry tactics such as controlled burns. This project will study how bush rats react to controlled burns and use that information to create welfare-focused guidelines that minimize impacts on wild rodent welfare. These guidelines could also help reduce the wild animal suffering caused by unplanned/naturogenic wildfires.

  • Does diet mediate effects of sublethal parasitic infections on host welfare?: This project is primarily studying the impact of intestinal nematode parasites on wild mouse welfare and how that effect interacts with other risk factors. However, because it takes an experimental approach by deworming some of the mice in expectation of seeing a positive welfare impact, it could also be considered a trial of a wild animal welfare intervention.

     

Figure 1: How WAI’s grantmaking has broken out across taxa (note that rodents are distinguished as a priority group from non-rodent mammals), project types, and welfare factor categories since our 2023 calls for proposals (which is when our metrics became more consistent). It reflects the consequences of some meaningful prioritization decisions on our part: 1) lots of funding to rodent projects; 2) significant funding to invertebrate projects and almost all of it to projects whose primary purpose is "measuring welfare" (because that remains the primary barrier to understanding and improving invertebrate welfare, even more than with other taxa); 3) generally diversified funding across taxa and welfare factors. These reflect our strategy of building and maintaining a broad field that is working towards a better world for all animals, while nudging its priorities towards the most numerous animals and the most important and tractable causes of suffering. Note that for projects that considered welfare factors from multiple categories, the budget was divided equally across those categories.

 

What we haven’t seen enough of

We are happy with the foundation of wild animal welfare research we’ve seeded over the past few years, and excited to see those projects’ results. However, as I alluded to earlier, most of our early grantmaking took a big-tent, experimental approach, emphasizing giving a shot to scientists who were new to the field (which was almost everyone at the beginning) and initiating projects on diverse species using diverse methods. There is necessarily a trade-off, and that brings me to the topic of what we haven’t optimized for up to this point but need to see more of going forward. We haven’t seen enough projects building on each other. I mentioned one standout example above, which is the project using machine learning to evaluate attention bias in wild fish. However, this is one of a handful of exceptions.

The long timescale of academic research is probably a huge factor. From the point when we fund a project, it usually takes months to start; sometimes because the principal investigator must recruit a PhD student or postdoc, or permits must be obtained. Then, the pace of many projects is limited by field seasons. Once the data is collected, the pace of analysis and writing is largely in the hands of the researchers, but it is challenging, often requiring coordination of a whole team of researchers who may have other projects or teaching responsibilities. Then, there’s the academic publishing process, which is genuinely inefficient (to put it mildly). The net result of this is that most of the projects WAI has funded have not published their results yet, and the ones that have are mostly from the earliest funding rounds, when we funded projects on the widest variety of themes and methods. Funding wide early was a strategic choice, since our first priority was introducing new people to the field and demonstrating its scope and relevance across many disciplines. However, all this means that there has been little opportunity for new grant applicants to build on or even learn about previous WAI-funded research unless they already collaborate with the relevant grantees. Moreover, each year we’ve received a larger share of projects focusing on abundant/neglected taxa and more important causes of suffering, and we’ve generally prioritized those over continuing to fund less impactful research directions. We’re really pleased to be seeing that shift and think we’ve taken the right approach so far, but we are approaching a pivot point. Ultimately, it is crucial for projects to build on each other and develop into deep research programs because actually improving wild animal welfare is such a complex, multi-step challenge.

  

The next phase of WAI’s strategy

If our initial priority of establishing mainstream acceptance of WAWS was phase 1 of WAI’s strategy (~2019-2023), and phase 2 involved emphasizing the distinctiveness of the field by leaning more into our priority themes while still focusing on growing the field (~2023-26), we are now entering a third phase. To accelerate progress improving wild animal welfare by building on this initial foundation of research initiatives, and to encourage long-term commitment to WAWS by reinvesting in the researchers who have demonstrated enthusiasm and aptitude for WAWS, the next phase of WAI’s strategy will emphasize the development of research programs over individual projects, and developing institutions through networks of researchers.

We have lots of plans and changes in store to address those objectives. I won’t share anything here that we aren’t prepared to share with the scientists in our network, but I can describe some of the most important changes that will be coming to our grants program when our next call for proposals launches this fall. Currently, we offer three main types of research grants that are primarily distinguished by their budget limits and competitiveness. We are now introducing all-new grant types, with much more specific purposes. These grant types will be offered simultaneously, but are designed to lead from one type to the next for any given research program or study system:

  • The first stage will be a Seed Grant (<$30k), which are for observational or pilot studies intended to identify candidate welfare indicators that could be subjected to a more rigorous validation experiment. For example, I have rescued dozens of injured garden snails, and I’ve noticed a few things that might be relevant to welfare: the posture and rigidity of their eye stalks seems to vary depending on the circumstances, and how much they retract their body into their shells when they sleep seems to vary among individuals. Those hypotheses aren’t developed or grounded enough to warrant a validation experiment, but with a Seed Grant I could quantify those snail behaviors alongside welfare-relevant conditions (such as competition or parasite load) to look for statistical associations as a first step. (Incidentally, we recently funded a welfare indicator validation project for snails!)
  • For better-understood taxa and contexts, a Seed Grant may not be necessary and a researcher can proceed directly to the first major grant type, a Validation Grant (<$200k). These projects will be entirely focused on testing the validity of potential welfare indicators through a structured process originally proposed by Heather Browning and applied by WAI’s Research Manager Michaël Beaulieu and others (e.g. Beaulieu 2024). The validation process is absolutely essential for truly understanding wild animal welfare because it confirms that we are actually assessing welfare. However, it is highly rigorous, and we’ve found that many grant applicants understandably want to skip ahead to the more interesting and motivating questions. That’s why we’re introducing a specific grant type dedicated to this kind of project.
  • We are also tightening our requirements for projects’ welfare assessment frameworks, which will give grantees who successfully deliver on a validation project a distinct advantage if they subsequently propose to address those more interesting questions via the next grant type, a Welfare Ecology Grant (<$200k). These grants will focus on assessing how wild animal welfare is affected by ecological factors, such as resource availability, disease, etc., within particular ecosystems. The objective of these grants is to gradually build up a picture of the causal network of factors so that interventions or policies can eventually be devised to improve wild animal welfare.
  • Intervention Grants will support that final step, and will debut next year, with our 2027 call for proposals. These projects will run field trials of interventions based on justified hypotheses and monitoring and evaluation tools of the sort developed through Validation Grants and Welfare Ecology Grants. Currently, we do not have these pieces in place for any wild animal welfare intervention, although we have funded projects working towards a foundation for testing a few potential interventions, including rodent fertility control and bird feeding. Between now and the launch of Intervention Grants, WAI’s research team will also be developing a new internal research agenda for 2027-29 by working backwards from potential wild animal welfare interventions to identify recurring research questions that would need to be answered in order to recommend for or against multiple specific interventions. Our internal research agenda will focus on broad conceptual or methodological questions that emerge, but other lessons from this process will inform what we ask of future Intervention Grant applicants.

 

Figure 2: The progression path through WAI grant types. A grant applicant seeking to break ground on a new research program would first apply for a Seed Grant if their focal species and the welfare challenges they face are poorly understood. If the basic biology of the species is reasonably well understood, but it has not been studied in welfare terms in the wild, they may apply directly for a Validation Grant. If the applicant is already an experienced wild animal welfare scientist (based on publication record) and there are validated indicators for the proposed focal species (or close relatives), they may apply directly for a Welfare Ecology Grant. We expect that it will take multiple Welfare Ecology Grant projects (by the same or different teams) for most research programs to mature to the point where they can proceed to an Intervention Grant.

 

We will also be experimenting with ways to hasten the handover of new knowledge between projects, such as requiring grantees to commit to a timeline for publication (or at least pre-print sharing) and facilitating more small-scale meet-ups for researchers working on related problems (like this one organized by WAI grantees working on applying cognitive bias tests to wild animals). Investing in WAWS institutions, particularly research centers, could also help accelerate research feedback loops, since co-located wild animal welfare scientists should be relatively up-to-date with each other’s findings.

Conclusion

WAI’s first 7 years of field-building for wild animal welfare science has laid the foundations of a recognized and growing field (albeit one still almost fully dependent on WAI for funding). We have prioritized establishing awareness and legitimacy for the field, publishing research that articulates key concepts of the field, and awarding research grants that showcase the scope and priorities of the field while giving scientists from adjacent fields an opportunity to incorporate wild animal welfare into their personal research programs. A trade-off of this approach is that research has been less concentrated towards any single breakthrough or intervention. However, we are already seeing this pay off in terms of a broad base of interest and support for wild animal welfare science. Our grants have seeded many compelling avenues for further development, and we think the field has reached a stage where WAI-funded research effort can become more consolidated into projects that build on one another. This is a tactical evolution to help ensure the coordination-related benefits of an academic field are actually realized in terms of research towards the most pressing and action-relevant questions.
